newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai T-bill repo rates, spots close mostly up.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai T-bill repo rates, spots close mostly up.

text.p: Contracts on the treasury bill repurchase market in Shanghai closed mostly up on Wednesday on a technical rebound after recent falls, traders said.
The annual rate for the most actively traded seven-day contract rose to 8.00 percent from 5.01 percent on Monday.
Total turnover of the six-contract market rose to 1.8 million lots from 1.2 million lots.
One lot is 1,000 yuan face value of treasury bills.
Traders said the repo rates had hit low levels after falls in the past few days and that a technical rebound on Wednesday had been expected.
A rebound on the domestic A share markets in the past two days also supported the rates on Wednesday, they said.
"The rebound particularly supported the early-maturing three-day and seven-day contracts," one local trader said.
Traders said trading volume remained thin due to the impact of the withdrawal recently of state banks from the market.

The Shanghai Securities News said on Wednesday that state debt trading turnover on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges fell by about a half in June against May after Beijing banned state banks from trading state debt contracts on the exchanges and on regional trading centres.
Traders said they expected the repo rates to continue to rise on Thursday, though slightly.

Contracts on the T-bill spot market in Shanghai ended mostly up on Wednesday on improved market sentiment after rises in the past two weeks on the back of liquidity inflow from the weak stock markets, traders said.
The most actively traded 10-year bond that matures in June 2006 rose slightly to 110.62 yuan from 110.58 yuan.
Combined volume of the eight-contract market rose to 1.04 million lots from 697,743 lots.
Despite Wednesday's rise, traders said they believed the spot contracts would shortly see a technical correction after successive gains.
But in the mid-term, the contracts had potential to rise further due to their high yields and an expectation that the stock markets would continue to weaken, they said.
